definition: Preemption is a doctrine under which one law supersedes another law that would otherwise apply. In U.S. constitutional law, the term most often describes federal law superseding state law under the Supremacy Clause of Article VI, which makes the U.S. Constitution, valid federal statutes, and treaties, the supreme law of the land. Valid federal regulations issued under delegated authority can also have preemptive effect, see: Federal Savings & Loan Association et al. v. de la Cuesta, 458 U.S. 141 (1982). Federal law does not automatically replace state law merely because both address the same subject; there must be a recognized basis for the displacement. Federal Preemption Congress may preempt state law expressly by including a preemption clause in a statute. Preemption may also be implied. Field preemption exists when Congress intended federal law to occupy an entire regulatory field, leaving no room for state regulation even if the state rule complements federal law. Conflict preemption exists under two scenarios: impossibility and obstacles. Impossibility preemption occurs when compliance with both laws is not possible, and obstacle preemption occurs when a state law is an obstacle to the accomplishment and execution of the full purposes and objectives of a federal law. Courts examine the federal text, structure, and regulatory framework to identify the scope of any displacement. Whether federal law preempts a state rule depends on the particular federal source and the state law's operation.
